paper_metadata.title: Algorithm for pricing Asian-style FX options on a gate-based quantum computer

summary: The paper presents a gate-based quantum Monte Carlo method for pricing a EUR/PLN Asian call option with 4 observation dates, N=3 qubits per time point, and iterative amplitude estimation. Reported Table 1 values include classical MC prices of 554135.97, 333190.20, 140896.63, 32870.59, and 3579.75 across strikes 4.1639 to 5.0892, while Table 3 shows QAE min/avg/max results that are often much worse and highly unstable, e.g. 559535.99/589825.94/627083.38 at strike 4.1639 and 15685.7/27998.4/45607.69 at strike 5.0892.

experiments.description: Gate-based quantum Monte Carlo pricing of an Asian FX call option on EUR/PLN using distribution loading, QFT-based mean calculation, comparator, payoff encoding, and iterative amplitude estimation; evaluated on a simulator for multiple strikes and parameter settings.

algorithm.variant: Quantum Monte Carlo Asian option pricing with QFT-based adder and Iterative Amplitude Estimation (IAE)
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Not reported; distribution parameters and strike values are fixed from market data and experiment design.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Each EUR/PLN price at a time point is discretized into 2^N intervals using N=3 qubits per time point; the arithmetic mean is computed in a larger register using QFT-based addition; a comparator flags whether the averaged price exceeds the strike; payoff is encoded into an ancilla amplitude for amplitude estimation.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Price of an Asian call option: E[max(A_T - K, 0)] under the risk-neutral measure, with A_T = (1/M) sum_t S_t.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Comparator circuit sets a control qubit when S >= K; payoff is encoded via controlled Ry rotations; no penalty formulation.

problem_instance.description: EUR/PLN Asian call option pricing under a Black-Scholes-Merton model with time-dependent domestic/foreign rates and volatility; four observation dates and five strike values used for evaluation.

dataset_specification.description: Spot S0=4.6265; observation times 90/365, 182/365, 274/365, 365/365; rates and volatilities as reported in the paper.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Distribution generated from lognormal Black-Scholes-Merton dynamics; discretization interval chosen as low=mu-3sigma and high=mu+3sigma; prices mapped to 2^N bins; mean computed from discretized path values.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Comparison against classical Monte Carlo, discretization-only classical evaluation, statevector simulation, and QAE across five strikes; additional sensitivity study for c and N; results reported in tables.

implementation_details.classical_solver: Classical Monte Carlo; statevector simulator used to isolate discretization and payoff-approximation error; QAE used for probability extraction.
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Generate EUR/PLN path probabilities from lognormal BSM model; discretize prices into bins; compute classical benchmark prices.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Convert measured ancilla probability to option price using price = fmax * (p^{-1/2} + 1/2) as written in the paper.

results.unit: qubits per time point for distribution loading

speedup_claims.conditions: via amplitude estimation for Monte Carlo-style option pricing
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states the quadratic speed-up as a general claim from prior work; the reported experiments are simulator-based and do not demonstrate runtime speedup.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Quadratic speed-up over classical Monte Carlo is claimed via amplitude estimation; no full asymptotic derivation specific to this implementation is given.
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Monte Carlo error scales as O(sqrt(var(H(S))/M)) in the paper's discussion.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not established; the paper reports only simulator-based evaluation and no hardware resource scaling sufficient to support advantage.
limiting_factors: Only simulator/statevector and QAE experiments are reported, not a QPU demonstration
Classical Monte Carlo is the baseline and is more stable than QAE in the reported results
QAE outputs are highly unstable across runs (min/avg/max spread is large)
The claimed speedup is quadratic, which Hoefler-style constant-factor analysis generally deems non-viable on NISQ-era hardware
Distribution loading and amplitude estimation dominate the circuit complexity

notes: hardware.type inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper explicitly says it used Qiskit statevector simulator for some experiments and reports no real QPU device; the overall evaluation is on quantum simulator rather than hardware.

num_qubits not explicitly summarized as a single total in the paper; inferred from the described registers: 4 time points with N=3 qubits each for distribution loading, plus additional mean/payoff/ancilla registers, but exact total circuit width is not cleanly stated.
The paper compares against classical Monte Carlo and reports that statevector results are close for some strikes, but QAE is unstable and often far from classical values.
No practical quantum advantage is demonstrated; the work is an algorithmic simulator study.
